standard.title: Culture, religion and citizenship
standard.description: how culture and religion may influence individuals' and groups' perceptions and expressions of citizenship and their actions as citizens
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how Australia's secular democracy draws on diverse cultural origins including Christian and Western heritage, distinct First Nations Australian histories and cultures, and migrant communities (AC9HC7K04). They understand how values of freedom, respect, fairness and equality support social cohesion (AC9HC7K05). The gap this descriptor fills is the mechanism by which culture and religion shape how individuals and groups enact citizenship — moving from understanding Australia's diverse society to understanding how that diversity plays out in lived citizenship.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how culture and religion may influence individuals' and groups' perceptions and expressions of citizenship and their actions as citizens, including through multiple community memberships, collective identities and the distinctions between types of citizenship.

nodes.label: Multiple community memberships and citizenship expression
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how membership of multiple communities (cultural, faith, professional, sporting, social) shapes how individuals express and enact citizenship.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how membership of one type of community group influences how an individual might express citizenship, with a specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how people express different aspects of their personal identity through membership of multiple communities — cultural groups, faith groups, professional associations, trade unions, sporting and social clubs — and explain how this is reflected in expressions of citizenship such as community service, advocacy and collective action.
wider: Investigate how a specific cultural or faith community in Australia expresses active citizenship — what forms of civic action are valued, what issues they engage with, and how their expression reflects their collective identity
Examine how the civic actions of diaspora communities — communities maintaining cultural identity while living in Australia — may differ from those of Australian-born citizens
Investigate how professional associations (e.g. medical, legal, teaching bodies) exercise citizenship through advocacy and policy engagement
nodes.hinge_reason: If students reduce citizenship to formal legal status or voting, they cannot engage with the descriptor's core idea that culture and religion shape how citizenship is enacted. This conceptual shift — from citizenship as legal category to citizenship as lived practice shaped by identity — is the foundation for the rest of the descriptor.

response_modes.reason: The concept of citizenship-as-practice is only legible through examples. Widening across different community types prevents students from anchoring to a single type of community and generalising inappropriately.

success_criteria: Can identify at least two types of community membership and explain how each might shape an individual's expression of citizenship
Can give a specific example of a citizenship action that reflects a community membership identity

nodes.label: Collective identities in multicultural Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore the collective identities of several different groups in Australia's multicultural society, and examine how those identities are represented and perceived.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the collective identity of one group in Australia's multicultural society and explain how it is represented in public life.
nodes.typical_width: Explore the collective identities of several different groups in Australia's multicultural society — examining how these identities are formed, how they are represented (e.g. in media, cultural events, advocacy) and how they are perceived by others within Australian society.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australian collective identities — as owners of their respective nations — are represented and sometimes misrepresented in mainstream Australian media and public discourse
Investigate how a specific migrant community has maintained and adapted its collective identity in Australia — examining what has been preserved, what has changed and what tensions arise
Examine how the representation of collective identities in Australia's national symbols (flag, anthem, public holidays) reflects some groups and not others, and what debates this produces

response_modes.reason: Genuine understanding of how identity and citizenship intersect requires encounter with diverse groups. Widening across First Nations Australian identities, migrant community identities and other cultural groups prevents students from working with a single representative case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Australia's multicultural society is a rich context for exploring how collective identity and citizenship interact. Width across First Nations, migrant and other community identities — and how they are represented and perceived — builds civic literacy that students can apply to current events and debates.
success_criteria: Can describe the collective identity of at least one group in Australia's multicultural society
Can explain how that identity is represented in public life and how it may be perceived differently by different audiences

nodes.label: Types of citizenship: legal, active and global
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the distinctions between legal citizenship, active citizenship and global citizenship.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the difference between legal citizenship and active citizenship with a concrete example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss the distinctions between legal citizenship (formal membership of a nation-state and the rights/responsibilities it confers), active citizenship (engaged participation in civic and democratic life) and global citizenship (a sense of belonging to and responsibility toward a global community) — explaining how these categories can overlap and how culture and religion influence which forms of citizenship an individual prioritises.
wider: Investigate how global citizenship is expressed through specific international or transnational movements (e.g. climate action, human rights advocacy) and how this relates to national citizenship
Examine the relationship between legal and active citizenship — whether legal citizenship is necessary for active citizenship, with examples from Australia
Investigate how people whose cultural or religious identity is transnational (e.g. diaspora communities, global faith communities) navigate the relationship between global and national citizenship

response_modes.reason: This node integrates multiple community memberships and collective identity from the previous nodes into a framework for understanding citizenship in its fullest sense. Ensure students can apply all three citizenship categories to examples from earlier in the descriptor.

success_criteria: Can explain the distinction between legal, active and global citizenship
Can give an example of how culture or religion might lead an individual to prioritise one form of citizenship over another
